opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, from the inside it didn't feel like "success" at the time. It felt like a lot of uncertainty.

When I started at Stanford, I was working in formal methods, on things like SMT solving and automated reasoning. It's a very rigorous field. You're trying to prove that a system behaves correctly, and there's very little room for hand-waving. I think that shaped me a lot. It taught me to be precise, to think carefully about corner cases, and to be patient with problems that don't yield quickly.

But I also remember feeling a kind of tension. Papers were getting accepted and people around me were supportive, so from the outside it may have looked like things were going well. Inside, I kept asking myself whether this was the area where I could have the biggest impact. Formal methods is beautiful, but the feedback loop with the real world can be slow. You build something elegant, and it may take years before it meaningfully changes how people build systems.

Around that time, large language models were starting to take off, and I could feel the energy shifting. I was curious, and a bit anxious, because switching directions mid-PhD is risky. You're giving up some accumulated advantage and starting over as a beginner.

Looking back, I think the formal methods years were very valuable, even though I eventually moved toward ML systems. The habits carried over: thinking in terms of abstractions, caring about correctness, and designing systems carefully rather than just hacking until something works. When we later worked on serving and programming LLMs, that mindset helped a lot.

So I'd say the early success gave me confidence that I could do research. But the more important lesson was learning to be honest with myself about what I actually wanted to work on, and being willing to leave a comfortable path for one that felt more alive.

r001.rationale: It contrasts supportive outward signs with inner uncertainty, but does not describe the work as dry and boring; it calls formal methods rigorous and beautiful.

r002.rationale: It says she started in formal methods, but does not state when or how her interest in the field developed.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the IJCAR Best Paper award or say whether it affected her uncertainty about what to pursue next.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, from the inside it never felt like "success" at the time. It felt like a lot of staring at proofs that wouldn't close.

I came to Stanford wanting to work on formal methods because I liked the idea that you could say something about a system with certainty, not just "we tested it and it seemed fine." That appeal is very real when you're a student. You feel like you're building on bedrock.

But the day-to-day was humbling. The problems that look elegant in a paper are usually the product of months of wrong turns. I remember spending weeks on an encoding that I was sure would work, and the solver would just time out, over and over. You start to question whether you're the problem or the problem is the problem. Usually it's a bit of both.

What I think people outside see as early success was really two things. One, I had very good advisors and collaborators who were generous with their time, and who let me pursue ideas that weren't obviously going to pay off. Two, I got a bit lucky with timing. Verification tooling was maturing, and there was a window where a careful student could make a real contribution without needing a huge team.

If there's something I'd take from that period, it's that formal methods trained me to be honest about what I actually know versus what I hope is true. That mindset turned out to be more valuable than any specific result. When I later moved toward systems and large-scale ML infrastructure, where nothing is provably correct and everything is empirical, I kept asking "what is the invariant here, and what would break it?" That habit came straight from those years of fighting with provers.

So from the inside, it looked like slow, often frustrating work with a few moments where things finally clicked. The "success" label is something you only see in hindsight.

astra-6.text:
From the inside, it felt much less like “early success” and more like a process of figuring things out. When you look back, you can draw a neat line through the work, but while you’re doing research, you don’t know which ideas will lead somewhere.

What attracted me to formal methods was the possibility of making a precise argument about whether a system behaves the way we intend, rather than just observing that it works on some examples. But even with that clarity as a goal, the research process itself is uncertain. You have to find the right question, understand your assumptions, and be willing to revise your approach.

So I would be cautious about treating early results as evidence that I had everything figured out. I see them more as steps in learning how to do research.

sol-6.1.text:
From the inside, it felt much less like an early success and much more like a process of learning how to do research. You spend a lot of time being confused, trying an idea, and figuring out why it doesn’t work. When something finally comes together, other people see the result, but you remember all those intermediate steps.

For me, the appeal of formal methods is that you have to be precise: What exactly are you claiming, and under what assumptions does it hold? I think that’s also a useful way to look at your own progress. A good result matters, but it doesn’t mean you suddenly know how to solve every problem. You’re still learning.
